procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Sessions Judge Court No.1, Hathras
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 03.01.2023 passed by the High Court at Allahabad in Criminal Revision No.4235 of 2022, which dismissed the revision challenging the order passed under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. summoning the petitioners/appellants.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants approached the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad by way of Criminal Revision No.4235 of 2022, challenging the order of the Additional Sessions Judge. The High Court dismissed the revision and affirmed the order of the Additional Sessions Judge.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, aggrieved by the High Court's order, approached the Supreme Court by way of Criminal Appeal No. 2186 of 2023. The Supreme Court issued notice on 08.05.2023 and directed the matter to be listed in the second week of July, 2023.

issue.issue_text: Whether an accused, who is impleaded under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C., is entitled to file an application for discharge.

facts: The case does not concern specific facts but rather a pure question of law regarding the procedural rights of an accused person.
law: Section 319 of the Cr.P.C., which allows a court to summon an additional person as an accused during a trial based on evidence that emerges.
Section 227 of the Cr.P.C., which provides for the discharge of an accused if the court finds insufficient grounds to proceed against them.
Section 398 of the Cr.P.C., which grants revisional powers to the High Court or Sessions Judge to order further inquiry into the case of a discharged accused.
application: The Court addressed the central conflict between the nature of a Section 319 summons and the right to seek discharge under Section 227.

The Court considered the argument that a person summoned under Section 319 should not be entitled to discharge. This argument is based on the premise that the court has already applied a 'higher degree' of satisfaction based on trial evidence to summon the person, making a discharge application redundant.
This opposing view also holds that discharge is a pre-trial remedy, whereas a Section 319 summons occurs mid-trial.

However, the Supreme Court rejected this reasoning. By finding in favor of the accused's right ('accepted'), the Court affirmed the principle that any person facing trial as an accused is entitled to the full spectrum of procedural remedies available under the law.

The decision implies that the timing of a person's inclusion in a trial does not diminish their right to challenge the sufficiency of the grounds for their prosecution. The status of being an 'accused' is the key qualifier for seeking discharge, not whether they were an accused from the inception of the case or added later.
The text acknowledges that this was a contentious legal issue, previously identified as needing clarification by a larger bench, which supports the Court's re-evaluation of the matter.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an accused person who is impleaded in a case mid-trial under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. is entitled to file an application for discharge under Section 227 of the Cr.P.C.

issue.issue_text: Whether a person before being impleaded as an accused under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. is entitled to a prior hearing.

facts: The appellants, who were summoned to be added as accused under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C., argued that the summoning order was invalid because they were not given an opportunity to be heard beforehand.
They contended that principles of natural justice and certain previous court observations required that a person be heard before being impleaded under this section.
law: Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. empowers a court to proceed against any person not being the accused if it appears from the evidence that they have committed any offense for which they could be tried together with the accused.
The Court focused on the expression "to proceed" within Section 319, interpreting it to mean proceeding with the main trial without interruption.
application: The Supreme Court determined that a prior hearing is not a mandatory requirement or a pre-condition for summoning a person under Section 319 Cr.P.C.

The Court reasoned that the purpose of the section is to proceed with the ongoing trial, and granting a prior hearing would lead to a "mini trial or a trial within a trial." This would jeopardize and derail the main proceedings, especially against accused persons who are already facing trial.

It was held that a person summoned under Section 319 cannot be allowed to "hijack the trial" and deviate its focus. The procedure upon appearance is simply to ascertain the person's identity, not to conduct an inquiry into their involvement.

The Court clarified that the rights of the summoned person are not completely disregarded. They have the right to challenge the summoning order before a superior court and, once added as an accused, they will have the full opportunity to cross-examine witnesses and present their own defense evidence during the trial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention, holding that a person is not entitled to a prior hearing before being impleaded as an accused under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. The Court found that such a requirement is not mandated by the law and would improperly disrupt and delay the main criminal trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a person before being impleaded as an accused under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. is entitled to a prior hearing.
appellant_arguments: The appellants' primary argument, based on the precedent set in Jogendra Yadav vs. State of Bihar, was that they were entitled to an opportunity of being heard before being added as accused.
They contended that since no such prior hearing was provided to them, the order impleading them as accused should be set aside and the matter remanded to the Sessions Court for a fresh hearing.
respondent_arguments: The text implies the respondent argued against the requirement of a pre-summoning hearing, suggesting that the evidence against a person proposed to be summoned does not need to be tested by cross-examination at that stage.

cases.case_name: Sukhpal Singh Khair v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: A right of hearing must be afforded to a person before being summoned and added as an accused in the trial under Section 319 Cr.P.C.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Principles of natural justice cannot be applied in a strait-jacket formula; their application depends upon the facts of each case and the object and purpose to be achieved under a provision of law.
obiter: If a court is to take a view which is at variance with a previous judgment, the aspect must be gone into.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The principles of natural justice cannot be applied in a strait-jacket formula and do not mandate a prior hearing for a person being impleaded as an accused under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C.; however, such an accused person retains the remedy of seeking discharge at the appropriate stage of the proceedings.
legal_tests_applied: Principles of natural justice cannot be applied in strait-jacket formula and they would depend upon the facts of each case and the object and purpose to be achieved under a provision of law.
why_appellant_lost: The court held that the principles of natural justice are not absolute and do not automatically require a pre-summoning hearing, stating it is well settled that they 'cannot be applied in strait-jacket formula'.

The court rejected the argument that a hearing provided in some prior cases sets a mandatory precedent, reasoning that 'Merely because in certain proceedings the persons summoned had been provided an opportunity of being heard cannot be the same thing as stating that it is a mandatory' requirement.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position prevailed because the court affirmed that the flexible nature of natural justice principles does not necessitate a mandatory pre-summoning hearing under Section 319 Cr.P.C.

The court implicitly affirmed that the threshold for summoning is the court's opinion that 'there appears to be some evidence pointing to the complicity of some other persons,' not a mini-trial with the proposed accused.
policy_considerations: The court preserved a key procedural safeguard for the accused by clarifying that even without a pre-summoning hearing, the remedy of seeking discharge remains available, stating it 'would have been inclined to reserve the remedy of seeking discharge, if so advised at the appropriate stage.'
